name: Birthmark
summary: Not all birthmarks respond to treatment the same way.
leadAnswer: Birthmarks are marks present at or soon after birth, made either of clustered pigment cells (café-au-lait patches, naevus of Ota, Mongolian spots) or of blood vessels (port-wine stains, salmon patches, haemangiomas).
seoTitle: Birthmark Removal Assessment in Malaysia | Kaiteki
seoDescription: Birthmarks vary widely in type and cause, and most are harmless. A doctor examines yours before discussing birthmark removal. Book a free consultation.

banner.alt: Illustrative photograph: a woman with a brown birthmark on her cheek

facts.label: Pigment birthmarks and blood-vessel birthmarks respond to different laser energy.
Several common birthmarks fade on their own or are better monitored than treated.
A birthmark that grows, darkens, bleeds or becomes raised should be examined.

sections.heading: What is a birthmark?
body: A birthmark is an area of skin that is discoloured from birth or appears in the first weeks of life.
Nothing a parent did or did not do during pregnancy causes a birthmark.

drivers.heading: What a doctor looks at first
drivers.intro: Three things decide whether a birthmark is a candidate for treatment at all, and which laser would even be relevant.

items.lead: Which structure it is made of.
items.body: Pigmented birthmarks come from clusters of melanocytes, the pigment cells in the upper layer of skin. Vascular birthmarks come from blood vessels in the dermis below.

Pigment near the surface looks brown; pigment deeper in the dermis looks blue or grey. A slate-grey patch over an infant's lower back is usually a Mongolian spot, which is common in Asian babies and normally fades during childhood without treatment.
A mole or mark that is growing, darkening or becoming raised is examined and monitored rather than lasered, because laser can hide the changes a doctor needs to see.

figures.caption: Cross-section of skin: pigment cells (melanocytes) sit in the upper layer, blood vessels deeper in the dermis. Diagram: National Cancer Institute, public domain.
A slate-grey Mongolian spot on an infant's lower back. Photo: abby lu, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

variant.heading: Which type is it?
variant.intro: Some marks belong to neither treatment route.

tabs.label: Pigmented
tabs.title: Pigmented birthmarks
tabs.body: Flat patches that are light to dark brown, or blue-grey where the pigment sits deeper. Café-au-lait patches, naevus of Ota around the eye and temple, and Mongolian spots that persist past childhood all belong here.
tabs.routing: assessed for pigment laser, with a test area often discussed first.

tabs.label: Vascular
tabs.title: Vascular birthmarks
tabs.body: Marks made of blood vessels: flat pink-to-purple port-wine stains, paler salmon patches, and raised haemangiomas in infancy. Port-wine stains persist and can darken or thicken with age, which is one reason adults seek treatment for them.

items.body: the colour often fades briefly when pressed, and may look darker when warm, crying or exercising.

tabs.routing: assessed for vascular laser, or referred to a paediatric specialist where an infant haemangioma is involved.

tabs.label: Monitor
tabs.title: Marks to watch, not laser
tabs.body: Congenital moles, and any birthmark that has started to change, sit outside the cosmetic route.
tabs.routing: assessed and photographed for monitoring, with referral where anything looks atypical.

cards.title: Around the eye and temple
cards.body: A blue-grey or brown patch here in an adult is often naevus of Ota. Treatment near the eye uses protective eye shields and extra care, and the eye itself is sometimes checked as part of the assessment.

cards.title: Cheek and side of the face
cards.body: Port-wine stains and café-au-lait patches are common here.

cards.title: Forehead, eyelids and nape
cards.body: Salmon patches in babies: those on the face commonly fade; those on the nape more often persist.

cards.title: Lower back and buttocks
cards.body: The usual site for Mongolian spots, which normally fade in childhood.

cards.title: Trunk and limbs
cards.body: Café-au-lait patches and congenital moles are frequently found here.

note.title: Several patches, or a mark across the forehead and eyelid?
note.body: Six or more café-au-lait patches, or a port-wine stain over the forehead and upper eyelid, can occasionally be linked to conditions affecting other parts of the body. These are referred for medical assessment before any cosmetic treatment is discussed.

seeDoctor.heading: When to see a doctor
seeDoctor.intro: Most birthmarks are harmless and stay that way. These are the reasons to have one examined:
triggers: It is growing, changing shape, or developing an irregular or blurred edge.
The colour has changed, darkened unevenly, or now has several shades in it.
It has become raised, lumpy, itchy, crusted, or bleeds without an obvious injury.
A new pigmented mark has appeared in adulthood that you did not have before.
An infant's haemangioma is growing quickly, is near the eye, nose, lip or nappy area, or has broken down into a sore.

ctaMid.heading: Not sure whether yours is pigment or blood vessels?
ctaMid.body: Send us a photo on WhatsApp and a doctor can tell you what it looks like and whether it is worth an in-person assessment.

treatmentsIntro: Birthmark treatment depends on which structure the mark is made of. Pigmented and vascular birthmarks are treated with different lasers, and some birthmarks are not treated at all.

pico-laser.why: For pigment birthmarks such as naevus of Ota
pico-laser.body: Very short laser pulses break up pigment in the skin so the body can gradually clear it.

vascular-pigment-laser.why: For port-wine stains and other vessel birthmarks
vascular-pigment-laser.body: Laser energy absorbed by the blood in the vessels heats and closes them, lightening the colour of a vascular birthmark.

firstVisit.intro: The doctor checks whether the colour blanches under pressure, which tells pigment from blood vessels.

steps.title: History
steps.body: When the mark first appeared, whether it has changed, and any previous treatment.

steps.title: Examination
steps.body: Colour, depth, texture and edge, often under magnification.

steps.title: Photographs
steps.body: Standardised photographs give a fixed record for judging change.

steps.title: Discussion and plan
steps.body: What the mark most likely is, which laser if any, and whether referral is needed.

visitImages.caption: A vascular laser in use. Its wavelength targets blood vessels, which is why it is used for red and purple marks.
Some small marks are treated with a fine laser handpiece that works on a very small area at a time.

items.body: Redness, swelling and stinging after a session, and with vascular laser, purple-grey bruising over the treated area that can last one to two weeks. Small crusts or blisters can form and should be left to heal on their own.

Darkening (post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation) or lightening of the treated skin is possible with any laser, and is more likely in darker skin types and with sun exposure around treatment. It usually fades over months but can occasionally persist.
Scarring, a change in skin texture, and patchy or uneven lightening that leaves the mark looking mottled.

Laser cannot promise complete removal of any birthmark. Some types, café-au-lait patches in particular, can return after lightening, and port-wine stains are usually lightened rather than cleared. Laser is not used to remove congenital moles for appearance, and it does not change the underlying tendency that formed the mark.

risks.disclose: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, take medication that makes skin sensitive to light, have a tendency to keloid or raised scars, have had recent sun exposure or a tan, or have had previous treatment on the birthmark.

costFactors.intro: Pricing is set after assessment. It depends on:
factors: The type of birthmark, since pigmented and vascular marks are treated with different lasers.
The size of the area and where it sits, because marks near the eye take more time and care.
Whether a test area is done first, which is common on the face and on darker skin.
How many sessions are planned, which varies widely between types and is reviewed as the mark responds.

faqs.a: It depends on the type, and outcomes vary between individuals. Some pigmented birthmarks, such as naevus of Ota, often lighten with a course of pigment laser, and port-wine stains are commonly lightened with vascular laser.

faqs.q: Will my child's birthmark fade on its own?
faqs.a: Many do. Mongolian spots usually fade during childhood, salmon patches on the face often fade in the first years, and infant haemangiomas typically grow for several months before slowly shrinking. Port-wine stains and café-au-lait patches generally persist.

faqs.q: How many sessions does birthmark laser take?
faqs.a: There is no standard number, because it depends on the type, depth, size and location of the mark and on how your skin responds.
Most people describe a snapping or stinging sensation, like a rubber band flicked against the skin. Numbing cream and skin cooling are commonly used to make sessions more comfortable.

faqs.q: Can a birthmark come back after laser?
faqs.a: Some can. Café-au-lait patches in particular may darken again after initial lightening, and port-wine stains can slowly re-darken over years. Sun exposure makes both more likely.

faqs.q: Can a mole I was born with be lasered off?
faqs.a: Laser is not used to remove congenital moles for appearance. It can lighten the surface while leaving cells deeper down, which makes future changes harder to spot.

relatedConcerns.reason: Pigment birthmarks and acquired pigmentation are told apart at the same assessment.
Port-wine stains share their treatment approach with visible facial vessels.
Pico laser targets birthmark pigment and tattoo ink by a similar mechanism.
